accessibility.scope: This statement also covers our election-forecast site, <elections>elections.daatan.com</elections>. That site has not been audited separately yet; report a barrier there to the same address.
accessibility.body: We're working toward <wcag>WCAG 2.0</wcag> Level AA conformance (the basis of Israeli Standard IS 5568), but we're not there yet — we'd call it partially conformant. So far we've added a skip-to-content link, visible keyboard-focus indicators, labels for screen readers on form controls and icon buttons, fixed several color-contrast issues, and re-enabled pinch-to-zoom on mobile, but plenty of the site hasn't been individually audited yet. If you hit a barrier, please tell us — email our accessibility coordinator at <email>{emailAddress}</email> and we'll look into it.

meta.title: Who Saw 64 Seats Coming — Retro Analysis
meta.description: 1,100 statements from the six months before Israel’s November 2022 Knesset election, each rated for how likely its speaker thought a 61-seat majority for Netanyahu’s bloc was.

retroIsrael.lead: The six months before Israel’s 25th Knesset election: {count} statements from the Israeli press in Hebrew, English, Russian and Arabic, world media and think tanks. Each article was read in full and rated on one question: how likely did its main voice think it was that Netanyahu’s bloc (Likud, Religious Zionism, Shas, United Torah Judaism) would win 61 seats? The bloc won 64.
retroIsrael.ratingsNote: These are ratings, not stated odds. An AI model (Claude Haiku 4.5) reads each article and assigns P = 0.5 + 0.5 × stance; the speaker did not necessarily name a probability. P ≥ 0.6 counts as “expects”, P ≤ 0.4 as “does not”.
events: Bennett and Lapid announce the Knesset will dissolve
Knesset dissolved, Lapid becomes prime minister
Gantz and Sa’ar merge their parties
List deadline: the Joint List splits

polls.text: Share of October poll reports that left the bloc short of a majority. The most common figure was 60.
polls.metric: October poll reports with a seat total

media.text: Analysts and journalists split, but “no” came up more often: {no} against {yes}.

bloc.text: Likud and its partners promised 61, though many in the camp conceded the polls were a seat or two short.

anti.text: Lapid, Gantz and their allies ran on “Netanyahu has no 61”. Their mean P was {p}.

polls.intro: Each bubble counts poll reports that gave the bloc that many seats. For six months the median sat at 59–60, one or two short of a majority. On election day the bloc won 64: Meretz and Balad fell below the threshold and their votes were wasted.
polls.foot: {count} articles that give a seat total for the bloc. Several outlets often reported the same poll, so this measures weight in the news, not the number of distinct polls.
polls.aria: Seats given to Netanyahu’s bloc in poll reports, by month
polls.tip: {month}: {c, plural, one {# report} other {# reports}} with {seats} seats · month median {med}

trend.h: Six months of argument in one chart
trend.intro: Each dot is one article, placed at the probability of 61+ seats its main voice expressed. Each line is that group’s mean over the previous 14 days: what a reader could have seen at the time, without hindsight.
trend.foot: Full pool after filtering, {count} articles. The dashed line at 50% separates “more likely than not” from “less likely”. Hover the chart for the group means on a given day.
trend.aria: Mean probability of a 61-seat majority for Netanyahu’s bloc by group of voices, May to October 2022

voices.h: Who got it right, who didn’t
voices.intro: The clearest calls on both sides. The number is the probability we assigned. Quotes are checked against the article text; Hebrew and Arabic ones are translated.

split.intro: Share of positions by type of voice and by the outlet’s language. Politicians in both camps predictably said what suited them. The press split almost evenly, and language made little difference: Hebrew, Russian and Arabic outlets all leaned slightly towards deadlock.

table.intro: A balanced sample of the pool: at most 15 articles per outlet and 3 per speaker, polls capped at 30% and one per pollster a week, sceptics raised to 35% so their arguments stay visible. See how to read P.
table.langNote: Article titles, summaries and quotes in the table are shown in English, as extracted; original-language quotes are kept.

method.search: A seed list of 326 domains: news-indexer sources, the Israeli press in Hebrew, English, Russian and Arabic, world outlets, think tanks and pollsters. GDELT GKG via BigQuery returned 20,245 URLs from 157 of them. Israel Hayom, Haaretz English, NewsRu.co.il, INSS, JPPI and others missing from GDELT were added from the Wayback archive.
method.filter: Keywords in four languages, then Claude Haiku on titles: 2,261 of 8,780 candidates kept. Full texts then dropped irrelevant pieces, repeats of one speaker on one day, repeats of one pollster in one week, and anything edited after 1 November. Articles whose page date falls in an earlier campaign (2019–2021) were dropped, 37 of them. A second pass dropped 33 spring-2022 articles where “61” was about the current Knesset (no-confidence votes, defections, an alternative government), not the election. Dates were checked against the page itself.
method.rating: The model reads the text as of its publication date and returns the main voice’s stance from −1 to +1, confidence, the bloc’s seat total if given, and a verbatim quote. For seat polls the stance follows a fixed rule: ≤58 seats −0.6, 59 −0.4, 60 −0.2, 61–62 +0.3, ≥63 +0.6. The article’s framing can shift it by up to 0.2. The main voice is whoever the article quotes on the question, not the author.
method.m1: N12, Kan and Channel 13 are barely represented: their sites are absent from GDELT and Wayback lists their articles without titles. Israeli TV, where much of the forecasting happened, is not covered.
method.m2: About two thirds of Hebrew Israel Hayom articles for the window were fetched. Hebrew Haaretz, Walla and Ynet appear only through GDELT.
method.m3: 253 texts come from live pages and 47 from Wayback snapshots taken before 1 November.
method.m4: {unverified} of {total} quotes were not found verbatim in the text. They are model paraphrases and are flagged in the table.
method.m5: Ratings are by the model. It sometimes misplaces a speaker’s camp or reads a conditional “if Netanyahu gets 61” as a forecast, so some table rows are wrong. The cards above and about 40 rows were checked by hand.

retroIsrael.footer: DAATAN Retro-Analysis Archive · E02 · built 24 Sep 2026

numbers.intro: Every article gets one number, P: what its main voice expected at the time, before anyone knew the outcome.
numbers.def: The probability that Netanyahu’s bloc wins 61 or more seats, as the article’s main voice expressed it on the day of publication. 0 means “certainly not”, 1 means “certainly yes”, 0.5 means no view either way.
numbers.b1: The model rates the speaker’s stance from −1 to +1, and <m>P = 0.5 + 0.5 × stance</m>.
numbers.b2: A poll that gives the bloc 60 seats lands at P = 0.4, and 61–62 seats at 0.65. The article’s framing can move it by up to 0.1 in P.
numbers.b3: P ≥ 0.6 counts as “expects 61+” and P ≤ 0.4 as “doesn’t”. Mean P is the average over a group’s statements.

203.name: Nadav Eyal
203.role: Yedioth Ahronoth, translated in Al-Quds Al-Arabi
203.quote: Since the start of the campaign, Netanyahu has not been closer to victory than he is now, thanks to Sami Abu Shehada and his colleagues, of course.
203.note: Written three days after Balad left the Joint List. Balad fell below the threshold, and the wasted votes helped the bloc to its majority.

235.name: Amit Segal
235.role: Yedioth Ahronoth, reported by Kikar HaShabbat
235.quote: Netanyahu could theoretically reach 63 seats even if his camp wins less than half the votes.
235.note: He described the mechanism exactly. In the same piece he reported internal polls giving Netanyahu 59 (Lapid’s pollster) and 60.5 (Netanyahu’s own).

275.name: Yuval Karni
275.role: Yedioth Ahronoth, translated in Al-Quds Al-Arabi
275.quote: A 61-seat government headed by Netanyahu is the scenario with the highest likelihood of materializing.
275.note: Four days before the vote. His six scenarios also included deadlock and a sixth election.

90.name: Joel Rosenberg
90.quote: If I were a betting man at one of Trump’s casinos, I would probably put my money 60-40 on Netanyahu to come back.
90.note: One of the few explicit odds in the corpus, given in July, right after the Knesset dissolved. That is why P is 0.60.

37.name: Noga Tarnopolsky
37.quote: Netanyahu has no evident path back... the most likely outcome should the Bennett-Lapid coalition fall [is] additional cycles of inconclusive elections.
37.note: Published three days before the coalition did fall.

171.name: Ze’ev Elkin
171.quote: Netanyahu almost never reaches 61 seats in any poll... Netanyahu will not get 61 seats this time.
171.note: The core message of the Gantz–Sa’ar campaign. Said in Russian to Channel 7.

285.name: Bobby Ghosh
285.quote: The closest bet is holding a sixth election.

287.name: Shalom Lipner
287.quote: Even more likely than this bleak scenario materializing is the correspondingly precarious outcome of Israelis being dragged to another sixth ballot in a few months’ time.

meta.title: Who Saw February 24 Coming — Retro Analysis
meta.description: 910 statements from the three months before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, each rated for how likely its speaker thought the invasion was.

retroUkraine.lead: The three months before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine: {count} statements from world, Russian and Ukrainian media, think tanks and officials. Each article was read in full and rated on one question: how likely did its main voice think a full-scale invasion was, on the day it was published?
retroUkraine.ratingsNote: These are ratings, not stated odds. An AI model (Claude Haiku 4.5) reads each article and assigns P = 0.5 + 0.5 × stance; the speaker did not necessarily name a probability. P ≥ 0.6 counts as “expects”, P ≤ 0.4 as “does not”.
events: Budanov: attack likely in late January or early February
Russia publishes draft treaties with the US and NATO
Geneva talks, then NATO–Russia Council and OSCE
Sullivan: invasion could begin any day
Russia recognises the DNR and LNR

west.text: Western governments and intelligence services were nearly unanimous. Only {no} of their statements said no.

analysts.text: Experts and journalists mostly sided with Washington, but about one in {oneIn} did not believe in war.

ua.text: Kyiv was split. Military intelligence warned, while the Security Council and the President’s Office urged no panic.

ru.text: The Kremlin and the Foreign Ministry called invasion talk hysteria until the end. Their mean P was {p}.

trend.h: Three months of argument in one chart
trend.intro: Each dot is one article, placed at the invasion probability its main voice expressed. Each line is that group’s mean over the previous 14 days: what a reader could have seen at the time, without hindsight.
trend.foot: Full pool after filtering, {count} articles. The dashed line at 50% separates “more likely than not” from “less likely”. Hover the chart for the group means on a given day.
trend.aria: Mean invasion probability by group of voices, November 2021 to February 2022

voices.h: Who got it right, who didn’t
voices.intro: The clearest calls on both sides. The number is the invasion probability we assigned. Quotes are checked against the article text.

split.intro: Share of positions by type of voice and by the outlet’s country. Russian outlets are softer than their own government because they often relayed Western warnings, if only to rebut them. Ukrainian outlets barely differ from international ones.

table.intro: A balanced sample of the pool: at most 8 articles per outlet and 2 per speaker, with sceptics raised to 35% so their arguments stay visible. See how to read P.
table.langNote: Article titles, summaries and quotes in the table are shown in English, as extracted; original-language quotes are kept.

method.search: GDELT GKG via BigQuery over 122 domains: the sources news-indexer monitors, plus major world, Russian and Ukrainian outlets and think tanks. That gave 105,001 URLs. Gaps were filled from the Wayback archive, and key sceptics were found by hand.
method.filter: Title keywords kept 5,007 candidates, and Claude Haiku kept 2,432 of those on title alone. Full texts then dropped irrelevant pieces, repeats of one speaker on one day, and anything edited after 24 February. Dates were checked against the page itself.
method.rating: The model reads the text as of its publication date and returns the main voice’s stance from −1 to +1, confidence, expected scope and a verbatim quote. Expecting a Donbas-only operation caps P at 0.35, and limited strikes cap it at 0.45.
method.m1: FT, WSJ and Bloomberg are absent: GDELT lacks them for this window and they are paywalled. AP almost entirely collapsed in deduplication because it relays the same officials.
method.m2: We could not fetch the Metaculus forecast, Zelensky’s 28 January press conference, Fiona Hill’s NYT column, or Macron’s 8 February statement.
method.m3: 154 texts come from live pages and 46 from Wayback snapshots taken before 24 February. No signs of later edits were found in the live texts.
method.m4: {unverified} of {total} quotes were not found verbatim in the text. They are model paraphrases and are flagged in the table.
method.m5: Telegram, social media and broadcasts are not covered. Ratings are by the model, with about 60 rows checked by hand.

retroUkraine.footer: DAATAN Retro-Analysis Archive · E01 · built 23 Sep 2026

numbers.intro: Every article gets one number, P: what its main voice expected at the time, before anyone knew the outcome.
numbers.def: The probability of a full-scale invasion that the article’s main voice expressed on the day of publication. 0 means “certainly not”, 1 means “certainly yes”, 0.5 means no view either way.
numbers.b1: The model rates the speaker’s stance from −1 to +1, and <m>P = 0.5 + 0.5 × stance</m>.
numbers.b2: Expecting only a Donbas operation caps P at 0.35, and limited strikes cap it at 0.45. Those speakers did not predict what actually happened.
numbers.b3: P ≥ 0.6 counts as “expects it” and P ≤ 0.4 as “doesn’t”. Mean P is the average over a group’s statements.

1.name: Kyrylo Budanov
1.quote: Россия сосредоточила у границ Украины более 92 тыс. военнослужащих и готовится к нападению в конце января или начале февраля 2022 года.
1.note: Described a multi-axis assault three months out. Off on timing by about three weeks, right on scale.

125.name: Rob Lee
125.quote: …believes that a Russian military operation against Ukraine is more likely than not, in part because of the unprecedented scale of the Russian military buildup underway around the country.
125.note: The Washington Post paraphrasing his view. Lee tracked the buildup through open-source data.

151.name: Joe Biden
151.role: US President, quoted in The New York Times
151.quote: My guess is he will move in. He has to do something.
151.note: Said at the same 19 January press conference as the “minor incursion” remark. The P of 0.78 is the rating of the 2 February NYT analysis (Steven Erlanger) that quotes it, not of Biden himself.

158.name: Jonathan Finer
158.quote: Whatever Russian officials are saying in public about their intentions, we have to take that with a grain of salt because of what we’re actually seeing with our own eyes.

17.name: Dmitry Peskov
17.quote: Слова о якобы планируемом Россией нападении абсолютно беспочвенны.
17.note: “Talk of an allegedly planned Russian attack is absolutely groundless.” The line held until 21 February.

48.name: Institute for the Study of War
48.quote: Putin does not, in fact, intend to invade unoccupied Ukraine this winter despite the continued build-up of Russian forces in preparation to do so.
48.note: One of the few Western think tanks to say no outright.

86.name: Oleksiy Danilov
86.role: Secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council
86.quote: Сейчас угрозы открытой агрессии Российской Федерации против Украины не наблюдается… Поэтому отдыхайте спокойно, празднуйте.
86.note: “There is no threat of open aggression… So rest easy and celebrate.” A month earlier he had disputed Budanov’s warning.

120.name: Dmitri Trenin
120.quote: In the immediate future, say, the coming month, I think the answer is no.
120.note: Said on 20 January. The month ran out on 20 February, four days before the invasion.

129.name: Jeff Hawn
129.role: London School of Economics, in Foreign Policy
129.quote: While a full-scale invasion across Ukraine remains highly unlikely, there are a range of other options open to Russia.
129.note: The typical sceptic case: recognition of the republics or limited strikes would serve Moscow better.

meta.title: Who Saw $120 Oil and €200 Gas — Retro Analysis
meta.description: 264 rated articles from the six months before the February 2022 invasion, each rated for how likely its speaker thought Brent above $120 and TTF gas above €200/MWh were.

retroEnergy.lead: Six months before the invasion: {count} rated articles that quote banks, agencies, companies and the press on oil and European gas prices. Each was read in full and rated separately on two questions: would Brent settle at or above $120, and would TTF settle above €200/MWh in 2022. Both thresholds were crossed on 7 March 2022.
retroEnergy.ratingsNote: These are ratings, not stated odds. An AI model (Claude Haiku 4.5) reads each article and assigns P = 0.5 + 0.5 × position, unless the speaker named a probability; most articles name no price, so P is a directional reading. P ≥ 0.6 counts as “expects above”, P ≤ 0.4 as “does not”.

brent.text: Share of oil statements with P ≥ 0.6. Mean P across the whole pool {p}.

ttf.text: Share of gas statements with P ≥ 0.6. Mean P across the whole pool {p}.

agencies.text: Mean P of agencies on oil, {n} statements. {no} expected a price below the threshold: the EIA gave about $70-75 a barrel.

press.text: Share of press and analyst statements on gas with P ≥ 0.6, {n} statements. They expected a spike but most often named no number.
press.metric: press gas statements, share with P ≥ 0.6

prices.intro: The black line is the front-month futures price: Brent and TTF (Yahoo Finance series BZ=F and TTF=F). The red dashed line is the question threshold. The grey band is the window in which we collected statements; whatever lies to the right, the authors did not yet know.
prices.foot: Front-month closing prices (Yahoo Finance, BZ=F and TTF=F). Brent: 11 closes at or above $120 in 2022, peak $127.98 (8 March). TTF: 30 closes above €200, peak €339 (26 August).

who.intro: A dot is one article; its height is the probability the main voice expressed. The line is the group mean over the previous 30 days, shown when the group has at least four articles.
who.foot: The dashed line at 50% separates “more likely than not” from “less likely”. The chart stops at the invasion: later statements are not part of the question.
who.aria: Mean probability for {title} by group of voices, September 2021 to February 2022

voices.h: Who got it right, who did not
voices.intro: The clearest statements on each question. The number on the left is the probability we assigned to them. Quotes are checked against the article text.

split.h: Who said yes, who said no
split.intro: Shares of positions by type of main voice and by publication language. On oil, {agencyNo} of agency statements ({agencyN}) expected a price below the threshold; banks and the press were more mixed, though “does not expect” outnumbered “expects above” in both. On gas the corpus has {agencyGas} agency and {bankGas} bank statements; the press did most of the talking ({pressN}), and {pressY} of the time it expected a spike.

table.intro: A sample from the pool: up to 23 articles per outlet and up to 5 per speaker (the 15 and 3 caps were relaxed to fill the table). Articles rated “does not expect” or “uncertain” on at least one question were filled first: 66% of the table against 66% of the pool. One article can speak about both markets. See how to read P.
table.langNote: Article titles, summaries and quotes in the table are shown in English, as extracted; original-language quotes are kept.
table.mainVoiceSub: who is quoted, not the author

method.search: A list of 146 domains: business and energy press, agencies, banks, think tanks, and Russian-language and European outlets. GDELT GKG via BigQuery returned 12,432 distinct URLs with energy headlines. Bloomberg, the Financial Times and the Wall Street Journal were barely represented in GDELT for these topics (6 rows, 1 usable article).
method.filter: Keywords and Claude Haiku on headlines: 2,551 candidates were narrowed to 817. Full texts were downloaded; 496 got a rating. We dropped irrelevant items, articles that only describe prices, and articles with traces of edits after 24 February. Dates were checked against the page itself for every year, not only 2021-2022.
method.rating: The model reads the text as of the publication date and returns the main voice’s position from −1 to +1 separately for each question. When a price is named, a fixed rule applies: for example a Brent forecast below $90 gives −0.6, $105-119 gives −0.1, $130 and above gives +0.6; the article’s tone shifts it by at most 0.2. If the speaker stated a probability, that is used. For a range, the highest price the speaker treats as likely is used.
method.voice: P belongs to the article’s main voice, not to the outlet or the author: a TASS item on Gazprom’s words gets Gazprom’s P. P of 0.6 or more is “expects above the threshold”, P of 0.4 or less is “does not expect”.
gaps: Bloomberg, the Financial Times and the Wall Street Journal are barely represented: those sites barely appeared in GDELT for the topic, and what exists in Wayback is mostly paywalled.
Texts of 166 table articles come from live pages and 45 from the Wayback archive before 25 February. Live pages may have been edited, so articles with traces of later edits were dropped.

Most articles name neither a price nor a probability. For them P is the model’s reading: “the winter will be very hard” gives clearly above 0.5, but does not prove the author had EUR 200 in mind. P should not be read as a calibrated probability.

Ratings were set by a model. It sometimes mixes up the market (US gas instead of European) or takes a conditional scenario for a forecast. We removed by hand 12 articles whose TTF rating rested on US gas and 4 that held no forecast; other cases may remain. An independent check of 44 random rows against their texts found a defect in about half (95% CI 34-62%), a quarter of them changing what the dot says.

The price bands in the method are guidance for the model, not a mechanical formula: for a share of priced ratings P sits further from the band than the tone allowance permits (in the audit: 36% of priced Brent legs, before the clean-up). In the audit, recomputing P strictly by the rule lowered the Brent “expect above” share from about 28% to 17% and the TTF share from 62% to 54% (the TTF figure is from before the US-gas clean-up). Read the shares as direction, not as calibrated probabilities.
Brent here is the front-month future (Yahoo Finance BZ=F). Dated Brent spot on the same day, 8 March, was above $130, so a $130 threshold was not unambiguous; we used $120.
method.quotes: The opening (first 120 characters) of {unverified} of {total} quotes was not found in the text; they are marked in the table. A further 57 quotes are excerpts from two places in an article stitched with “...”; 113 quotes in all are not fully verbatim.

numbers.intro: Every article gets up to two numbers, P: what its main voice expected about each market at the time, before anyone knew the outcome.
numbers.def: One P for oil: the probability that Brent settles at or above $120 in 2022. One P for gas: that TTF settles above €200/MWh. The two are independent and never combined. 0 means “certainly not”, 1 means “certainly yes”, 0.5 means no view either way.
numbers.b1: The model rates the speaker’s position from −1 to +1, and <m>P = 0.5 + 0.5 × position</m>.
numbers.b2: Most articles name no price, so P is mostly directional: “prices will keep climbing” reads clearly above 0.5 without saying how high. It is not a calibrated probability.
numbers.b3: P ≥ 0.6 counts as “expects above the threshold” and P ≤ 0.4 as “does not”. Mean P is the average over a group’s statements.

160.name: JPMorgan
160.note: A conditional scenario, but with a number: $150. Published five weeks before the invasion.

206.name: Jeffrey Halley
206.note: Conditional on a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, said two days before it. Brent did close at or above $120 on 7 March.

120.name: Deutsche Bank
120.note: Among the lowest targets in the corpus ($60, shared with Standard Chartered and Moody’s). About fourteen weeks later Brent closed above $120.

152.name: EIA
152.note: The official forecast six weeks before the invasion. Brent averaged about $100 in 2022.

8.name: Alexey Miller
8.role: head of Gazprom, via Rossiyskaya Gazeta
8.note: The seller of the gas is speaking, and gives no number. P is high on direction, not on level.

164.name: Samantha Dart
164.note: A scenario view on possible flow disruption. €180 was the December high; the €200 line was crossed six weeks later.

167.name: ABN Amro
167.note: The right level, but the bank put the “Russia halts gas exports” scenario at 5-10%. The threshold was crossed without any halt.

5.name: Alexander Ivannikov
5.note: Three and a half months later, on 21 December, TTF closed at EUR 180, three times higher.

ukraine-2022.title: Who Saw the Invasion of Ukraine Coming
ukraine-2022.description: The three months before Russia’s full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022. Every statement was rated on how likely its speaker thought a full-scale invasion was, on the day it was published. Western governments averaged P = 80% (307 statements). Russian officials said no (P ≤ 0.4) in 80% of their 92 statements, and Ukrainian officials in 40% of their 92. P is a 0–1 rating of the invasion probability each statement implies, assigned by an AI model (Claude Haiku 4.5); it is not a number the speakers stated.

0.quote: Россия сосредоточила у границ Украины более 92 тыс. военнослужащих и готовится к нападению в конце января или начале февраля 2022 года.

1.quote: A Russian military operation against Ukraine is more likely than not, in part because of the unprecedented scale of the Russian military buildup underway around the country.

israel-2022.title: Who Saw 64 Seats Coming
israel-2022.description: The six months before Israel’s 25th Knesset election on 1 November 2022. Every statement was rated on how likely its speaker thought it was that Netanyahu’s bloc would win a 61-seat majority. Polls gave the bloc 59–60 seats throughout the campaign, and the press leaned towards deadlock and a sixth election. The bloc won 64. P is a 0–1 rating of the 61+ majority probability each statement implies, assigned by an AI model (Claude Haiku 4.5); it is not a number the speakers stated.

0.quote: If I were a betting man at one of Trump’s casinos, I would probably put my money 60-40 on Netanyahu to come back.

3.headline: Yuval Karni, Yedioth Ahronoth (translated)
3.quote: A 61-seat government headed by Netanyahu is the scenario with the highest likelihood of materializing.

energy-2022.title: Who Saw $120 Oil and €200 Gas
energy-2022.description: The six months before the February 2022 invasion. Every article was rated separately on two questions: would Brent settle at or above $120 and would TTF gas settle above €200/MWh in 2022. Both thresholds were crossed on 7 March 2022. Agencies mostly expected oil well below the line; the press expected a gas spike but rarely named a number. Most ratings are directional readings, not calibrated probabilities. P is a 0–1 rating of the probability each statement implies, assigned by an AI model (Claude Haiku 4.5), and the two markets are never combined.

0.headline: JPMorgan, bank
0.quote: International oil prices could soar to $150 a barrel during the first quarter of 2022 if an ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine leads to a supply shock.

1.headline: Jeffrey Halley, Oanda (if Russia invades in full)
1.quote: The immediate impact would be an exacerbation of the rampant inflationary pressures globally as oil hits $130.00+ a barrel.

2.headline: Alexey Miller, head of Gazprom
2.quote: The price of gas in Europe may break the already achieved records in the near future.

3.headline: Samantha Dart, Goldman Sachs
3.quote: We wouldn’t rule out in this scenario the market briefly revisiting the 180 EUR/MWh high observed in mid-December - or even higher levels.

0.headline: Deutsche Bank, bank
0.quote: Oil price may fall below $60 per barrel next year due to a significant increase in supply.

1.headline: U.S. Energy Information Administration
1.quote: We forecast that the price of Brent will average $75/b in 2022 and $68/b in 2023.

2.headline: ABN Amro, bank
2.quote: The TTF monthly contracts could trade above EUR 200/MWh for an extended period... Oil prices would be trading above $100/bbl. [ABN Amro put the scenario of a halt in Russian gas exports at 5-10%.]

3.headline: Alexander Ivannikov, Gazprom department head
3.quote: Gas prices in Europe will definitely remain at the current level in the near future.
